Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for agreeing to evaluate Ms. Clara Jenkins, a 23-year-old woman who recently transferred to my practice. She has a longstanding clinical history extending back to early childhood, around three years of age, when hematologic concerns were first documented.

Her recent laboratory evaluation demonstrates significant macrocytosis, with a hemoglobin of 8.7 g/dL and an MCV of 115 fL. The peripheral blood smear displays marked anisopoikilocytosis and hypersegmented granulocytes, indicating megaloblastic change. Accompanying metabolic studies demonstrated a profoundly low serum cobalamin level of 92 pg/mL. Additionally, routine urine studies revealed persistent dipstick-positive protein, with quantification confirming significant protein excretion, even though her serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen remain entirely within normal limits.

On examination today, she appears comfortable. Vital signs are normal, with a blood pressure of 116/74 mmHg and a pulse of 70 beats per minute. Neurological evaluation shows preserved vibratory sense and proprioception throughout the lower extremities, and cranial nerves are intact. Abdominal exam reveals no organomegaly, and cardiopulmonary auscultation is clear. She is currently employed as an archivist, does not smoke or drink alcohol, and takes only occasional paracetamol for headaches. Her family history is non-contributory.

Given the constellation of these laboratory findings dating from childhood, I would value your comprehensive evaluation and guidance regarding her diagnostic workup and ongoing management.

Sincerely,

Dr. Arthur Vance
Internal Medicine
